title: Everyone has an hour (Avot 4:3)
hook: despise no one and dismiss nothing; every person has their hour and every thing its place
tomorrow: why does one rabbi say 'very' twice?

segments.voice: Yesterday, one mitzvah brings another: the pay is more of the same. Ben Azzai's next line turns from deeds to people.

Every group chat has someone who barely posts, and every team has someone who stays on the bench. Ben Azzai has a word for them, and for us. Do not despise any person, he says, and do not dismiss any thing. For there is no person who doesn't have their hour, and no thing that doesn't have its place.
screen: `THE ONE WHO BARELY POSTS.` → `DESPISE NO ONE.` → `EVERYONE HAS AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Readers have heard this two ways, and both live inside the tradition. The first reading is respect. Every person matters now, whatever their hour; the hour is only when the rest of us finally notice. The Mishnah backs it elsewhere, in Sanhedrin: humanity began with a single person, it says, so that no one could ever tell another, my father is greater than yours. At its best: if everyone comes from one ancestor, there's no one left to look down on. The second reading is caution. Don't despise anyone, because their hour will come, and you may need them, or answer to them, when it does. At its best: it's honest about people, and humility about the future can still produce real respect. Ben Azzai's words hold both. Everyone has an hour can be a promise to the overlooked, or a warning to the proud. And the second half matters too: no thing without its place. Nothing in the world is junk, either.
screen: `TWO READINGS, ONE LINE.` · `RESPECT: ONE FIRST ANCESTOR.` · `CAUTION: THEIR HOUR WILL COME.` · `NO THING WITHOUT ITS PLACE.` · then, large: `EVERYONE HAS AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Look at one ordinary object near you: a chair, a cup, a light switch. Somebody you'll never meet designed it, made it, carried it, put it there. Let the sit be a quiet thank-you to the hands nobody saw.
Everyone has an hour. Ben Azzai's sha'ah: no person without their time, no thing without its place.
Your line: everyone has an hour. No person despised, and nothing dismissed. See you soon.
